titre: British civilisation: the UK since 1945 in 3 pages
essentiel: One storyline: Beveridge (1942) and Attlee (1945-1951) build the Welfare State and a mixed economy; both parties keep it (consensus, Butskellism) despite relative decline; the 1970s crisis ends the consensus; Thatcher (1979-1990) breaks with it (monetarism, privatisation, unions); Major and New Labour accept the market legacy and add social investment, devolution and peace in Northern Ireland.

chapitres.idee: A constitutional monarchy with an uncodified constitution, where Parliament is sovereign and the PM's power rests on a majority in the Commons won through first past the post.
points: Uncodified constitution: statutes, case law, conventions, historical documents (not 'no constitution')
Parliament = monarch + House of Commons (650 elected MPs) + House of Lords (unelected, delay limited by Parliament Acts 1911, 1949)
Parliamentary sovereignty: Parliament can pass or repeal any law
PM = leader of the majority party in the Commons; Cabinet collectively responsible; Opposition has a shadow cabinet
The monarch reigns but does not rule (Royal Assent, King's Speech)
FPTP in 650 constituencies: favours Conservatives and Labour, clear majorities on a minority of votes, punishes spread-out parties, helps the concentrated SNP

dates.fait: Labour back in power with a large majority

distinctions.difference: The UK has a constitution, spread across statutes, conventions and case law.

questions.q: Can a British PM change without a general election? Why?
questions.r: Yes: power rests on the majority in the Commons; if the party changes leader, the PM changes.

questions.q: What are the effects of first past the post?
questions.r: Two-party system, clear majorities on a minority of votes, spread-out parties (Lib Dems, Greens, Reform UK) under-represented, concentrated SNP favoured.

questions.q: Who sits in the House of Lords?
questions.r: Unelected members: appointed life peers, a limited number of hereditary peers, Church of England bishops.

chapitres.idee: The Liberal Beveridge Report (1942) gave the programme; Attlee's Labour government (1945-1951) built it: social insurance, a free tax-funded NHS and nationalisations.
points: Beveridge Report, Dec 1942 (Social Insurance and Allied Services): universal cover 'from the cradle to the grave'
Five giants: Want, Disease, Ignorance, Squalor, Idleness (= unemployment)
Flat-rate contributions for flat-rate benefits; assumes an NHS, family allowances, full employment
July 1945: Attlee's landslide over Churchill; 1946 National Insurance Act; 1948 National Assistance Act
NHS (Act 1946, launched 5 July 1948, Aneurin Bevan): free at the point of use, financed by taxation
Nationalisations in the name of Clause IV: about a fifth of the economy under public control (mixed economy)

dates.fait: Bank of England, aviation (1946); coal (1947); rail, electricity (1948); gas (1949); steel (1951)

distinctions.difference: Report written under the wartime coalition; Labour put it into practice.
Financed by taxation versus financed by contributions.

chapitres.memo: Five giants, five answers: Want-insurance, Disease-NHS, Ignorance-education, Squalor-housing, Idleness-full employment.

questions.q: Name Beveridge's five giants.
questions.r: Want, Disease, Ignorance, Squalor, Idleness.

questions.q: When and by whom was the NHS launched, and how is it financed?
questions.r: 5 July 1948, Aneurin Bevan (Attlee government); free at the point of use, financed by taxation.

questions.q: Why did Attlee nationalise?
questions.r: Clause IV (common ownership); modernise ageing industries, guarantee jobs, plan reconstruction.

chapitres.idee: 1951-1979: both parties share the Welfare State and Keynesianism (consensus) amid relative decline, until the 1970s crisis breaks the model.
points: Consensus: Welfare State and NHS, mixed economy, Keynesian full employment, consultation with unions
'Butskellism' (The Economist, 1954) = Butler (Con) + Gaitskell (Lab): continuity of economic policy
Relative decline: growth slower than West Germany, France, Japan; 'sick man of Europe' (1970s)
Stop-go: expansion -> inflation, external deficit -> pressure on sterling -> restraint -> unemployment -> expansion
Europe: ECSC/EEC turned down, EFTA (1960), de Gaulle's vetoes, accession 1973 (Heath), 1975 referendum about 67% Yes
1970s: miners' strikes, oil shock, three-day week, stagflation, IMF loan, Winter of Discontent

dates.fait: Winter of Discontent; no confidence vote March 1979; Thatcher wins May 1979

distinctions.difference: Living standards rise, but more slowly than neighbours'.

questions.q: What does Butskellism mean?
questions.r: Term from The Economist (1954): Butler + Gaitskell, the continuity of Conservative and Labour economic policy in the consensus.

questions.q: Explain the stop-go cycle.
questions.r: Boosting demand -> imports, inflation, deficit -> sterling under pressure -> restraint (interest rates, credit) -> slowdown -> new expansion.

questions.q: Why did the UK join Europe late?
questions.r: Priority to Commonwealth, US special relationship, sovereignty; applications in 1961 and 1967 vetoed by de Gaulle; entry 1973.

questions.q: What was the Winter of Discontent?
questions.r: 1978-1979: collapse of Labour's incomes policy, mass public sector strikes; Callaghan falls (March 1979), Thatcher wins (May 1979).

chapitres.idee: Thatcher (1979-1990) broke with the consensus: inflation before full employment, rolling back the state, privatisation, curbing the unions and deregulating the City.
points: Monetarism (Friedman, Hayek): control money supply (MTFS 1980), cut deficit, high interest rates; TINA, 'The lady's not for turning'
Cost: 1980-1981 recession, over 3 million unemployed, deindustrialised North; inflation falls by mid-1980s
Privatisation: efficiency, state revenue, weaker unions, 'popular capitalism'; Right to Buy (1980) = 'property-owning democracy'
Unions: Employment Acts 1980, 1982 (picketing, secondary action, closed shop); Trade Union Act 1984 (secret ballot)
Miners' strike March 1984 - March 1985 (NUM, Scargill), no national ballot, Orgreave: miners defeated
Big Bang 27 Oct 1986: fixed commissions abolished, broker/jobber split ended, foreign banks, electronic trading
Downfall: poll tax (flat rate per adult), Europe divisions, Howe resigns, Heseltine challenge, she quits Nov 1990

dates.fait: BT / British Gas ('Tell Sid') / BA and Rolls-Royce

distinctions.difference: Targets inflation through money vs full employment through demand.
Changes the owner vs loosens the rules (e.g. Big Bang).
Union victory over Heath vs defeat by Thatcher.

questions.q: What is monetarism and its short-term cost?
questions.r: Priority to inflation via money supply control, spending cuts, high rates; 1980-1981 recession, over 3 million unemployed.

questions.q: Give four privatisations with dates.
questions.r: BT 1984, British Gas 1986, BA and Rolls-Royce 1987, water 1989 (electricity 1990-1991).

questions.q: How did Thatcher fall?
questions.r: Not by election: poll tax anger, Europe divisions, Howe's resignation speech, Heseltine's challenge; she withdrew in Nov 1990, Major succeeded.

chapitres.idee: Major's weakened Conservatives (1990-1997) gave way to Blair's New Labour, which kept the Thatcherite market legacy while adding social investment, devolution and peace in Northern Ireland.
points: Major: council tax, Gulf War (1991), 1992 win, Black Wednesday (16 Sept 1992) = exit from the ERM, credibility lost
Major: Maastricht split (opt-outs: single currency, Social Chapter), sleaze, rail privatisation, Downing Street Declaration (1993)
Blair leader 1994; Clause IV rewritten 1995; Third Way (Giddens): market + education, health, welfare to work
1997-1998: Bank of England independence, minimum wage, Human Rights Act; tarnished by Iraq (2003); Brown 2007
Devolution: powers transferred, Westminster stays sovereign (unitary state); West Lothian question
Good Friday Agreement: consent principle, power-sharing, North-South bodies, decommissioning, prisoner release

dates.fait: Devolution referendums (big Yes Scotland, narrow Yes Wales)
Good Friday Agreement signed; twin referendums 22 May 1998
Scottish Parliament (Holyrood) and Welsh Assembly (now Senedd) elected

distinctions.difference: Westminster remains sovereign vs guaranteed shared sovereignty.
Market + social investment vs nationalisation and unions.

questions.q: What was Black Wednesday and its consequence?
questions.r: 16 Sept 1992: sterling forced out of the ERM; Conservatives lose economic credibility.

questions.q: Define the Third Way.
questions.r: Giddens: beyond state socialism and neoliberalism; accept the market and Thatcher legacy, invest in education, health, welfare to work.

questions.q: What is the West Lothian question?
questions.r: Scottish MPs at Westminster vote on laws that concern only England.

questions.q: Main principles of the Good Friday Agreement?
questions.r: Consent of the majority, power-sharing Assembly and Executive, North-South and East-West bodies, decommissioning, prisoner release.

chapitres.idee: A commentary presents, explains and interprets a document in its historical context: outside knowledge and critical distance, never paraphrase.
points: Identify: nature, author, date, source, audience
Contextualise the political, economic and social situation
Central question on the document's historical interest
Thematic outline in 2-3 parts (not line by line)
Short quotations with line numbers + precise knowledge (dates, laws, actors)
Significance and limits: point of view, intentions, omissions; conclusion answers the question and opens
chapitres.memo: Present, Place, Problem, Plan, Prove, Perspective.

questions.q: What goes into the introduction?
questions.r: Presentation (nature, author, date, source, audience, context), central question, outline.

questions.q: Give a central question for Thatcher's 1980 conference speech.
questions.r: How does this speech assert Thatcherism's break with the post-war consensus?

questions.q: Two phrases to criticise a document?
questions.r: 'However, the author fails to mention...' / 'This view should be qualified...'

parCoeur: 1942 Beveridge Report; five giants: Want, Disease, Ignorance, Squalor, Idleness
July 1945 Attlee wins; 5 July 1948 NHS (Bevan), free, tax-funded
Butskellism (1954) = Butler + Gaitskell: consensus on Welfare State, mixed economy, Keynesianism
Devaluations 1949 and 1967; stop-go; 'sick man of Europe'
Europe: EFTA 1960, vetoes 1963 and 1967, entry 1 Jan 1973, referendum 1975 (about 67% Yes), Brexit 2016/2020
Crisis: three-day week 1974, IMF 1976, Winter of Discontent 1978-1979, Thatcher May 1979
Privatisations: BT 1984, Gas 1986, BA 1987, water 1989, electricity 1990-1991; Right to Buy 1980
Miners' strike March 1984 - March 1985; Big Bang 27 Oct 1986; Thatcher resigns Nov 1990
Black Wednesday 16 Sept 1992; Maastricht ratified 1993; New Labour 1 May 1997
Clause IV rewritten 1995; Bank of England independent 1997; minimum wage and Human Rights Act 1998
Good Friday Agreement 10 April 1998 (referendums 22 May); devolved bodies elected 1999
Commons: 650 MPs, FPTP; Parliament Acts 1911, 1949 limit the Lords
pieges: Saying the UK has 'no constitution': it is uncodified, not absent.
Crediting the Beveridge Report to Labour: Beveridge was a Liberal under the wartime coalition; Attlee implemented it.
Confusing the Winter of Discontent (1978-1979, Callaghan) with the miners' strike (1984-1985, Thatcher), or the 1974 strike (won) with 1984-1985 (lost).
Saying Thatcher lost an election: she was ousted by her own party in Nov 1990.
Confusing privatisation (owner changes) with deregulation (rules loosened), or devolution with federalism.
Paraphrasing the document instead of explaining it with outside knowledge and a thematic outline.
